issues.legal_issue: The relationship of an eyewitness to an accused, without more, does not make the eyewitness’s testimony unreliable.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses included close relatives of the injured persons and were said to be on inimical terms with the accused because of a property dispute.
The courts below found the evidence against the appellants cogent and credible.
No adequate foundation was laid for the claim that the witnesses had falsely implicated the appellants.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ relationship to the injured persons and alleged hostility did not, by themselves, justify rejecting their testimony.
issues.legal_principle: A relative is not to be treated as an unreliable or partisan witness merely because of the relationship; the court must assess the evidence carefully and determine whether it is cogent and credible, and a claim of false implication requires a factual foundation. The Court relied on Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1953 SC 364; Guli Chand v. State of Rajasthan, (1974) 3 SCC 698; Vadivelu Thevar v. State of Madras, AIR 1957 SC 614; Rameshwar v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1957 SC 54; Masalti v. State of U.P., AIR 1965 SC 202; State of Punjab v. Jagir Singh, AIR 1973 SC 2407; and Lebna v. State of Haryana, (2002) 3 SCC 76.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and related_eyewitnesses and credible_testimony and not substantiated_false_implication

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed against criminal convictions.
predicates.related_eyewitnesses: The prosecution relied on eyewitnesses who were related to the injured persons.
predicates.credible_testimony: The courts found the eyewitness testimony against the accused cogent and credible.
predicates.substantiated_false_implication: The accused provided a factual foundation for the claim that the witnesses falsely implicated them.
predicates.relationship_alone_does_not_discredit_te: The eyewitness testimony is not rejected solely because the eyewitnesses are related to the injured persons.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal challenges convictions based on credible testimony from related eyewitnesses, and false implication is not substantiated, the testimony is not discredited solely because of the relationship.

issues.legal_issue: Credible and separable evidence against some accused may sustain their convictions even when other accused are acquitted on the same prosecution case.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted several accused but convicted the appellants.
The courts below identified distinguishing features in the evidence concerning the acquitted and convicted accused.
The appellants argued that the acquittals required their convictions to be set aside.
issues.conclusion: The acquittals of other accused did not require the appellants’ convictions to be set aside because the evidence against the appellants was separately found sufficient and credible.
issues.legal_principle: The maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus is not a rule of law in India but a rule of caution; the court must assess the evidence and separate truth from falsehood where possible. A conviction can stand on the credible residue even if evidence against other accused is insufficient, provided the evidence can be separated without reconstructing an entirely new case. The Court relied on Nisar Alli v. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1957 SC 366; Gurcharan Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1956 SC 460; Sohrab v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (1972) 3 SCC 751; Ugar Ahir v. State of Bihar, AIR 1965 SC 277; Zwingle Ariel v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1954 SC 15; Balaka Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1962 SC; State of Rajasthan v. Smt. Kalki, AIR 1981 SC 1390; Krishna Mochi v. State of Bihar, JT 2002 (4) SC 186; and Gangadhar Behera v. State of Orissa, (2002) 7 Supreme 276.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and some_coaccused_acquitted and credible_evidence_against_appellant and evidence_is_separable

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed against a criminal conviction.
predicates.some_coaccused_acquitted: The trial court acquitted some people accused in the same prosecution.
predicates.credible_evidence_against_appellant: The courts found credible evidence establishing the appellant’s guilt.
predicates.evidence_is_separable: The evidence against the appellant can be distinguished from evidence that was insufficient against other accused.
predicates.conviction_may_stand_despite_coaccused_a: A conviction may remain in force despite acquittals of other accused in the same case.

issues.definition: When some co-accused are acquitted but credible evidence against the appellant is separable, the appellant’s conviction may stand.

issues.legal_issue: A claim of private defence must be supported by a reasonable and probable account of circumstances justifying the harm caused.
material_facts: The appellants claimed that they had acted in private defence.
The courts found that none of the accused had any injury, while the principal injured witness had numerous injuries and was hospitalised for more than a month.
The appellants did not establish circumstances making their private-defence account reasonably probable.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the private-defence claim and upheld the convictions.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 96–106 of the Indian Penal Code, the right of private defence depends on the circumstances, is limited by Section 99, and lasts only while a reasonable apprehension of danger continues; Sections 100–102 address its extent and commencement and continuance for the defence of the body. Under Section 105 of the Indian Evidence Act, the accused bears the burden of establishing the exception, but need only show a preponderance of probabilities, including through prosecution evidence. The defence must present a reasonable and probable account showing that the harm was necessary to ward off an attack or avert a continuing reasonable apprehension. Injuries to an accused are relevant but do not automatically establish private defence. The Court relied on Munshi Ram v. Delhi Administration, AIR 1968 SC 702; State of Gujarat v. Bal Fatima, AIR 1975 SC 1478; State of U.P. v. Mohd. Musheer Khan, AIR 1977 SC 2226; Mohinder Pal Jolly v. State of Punjab, AIR 1979 SC 577; Salim Zia v. State of U.P., AIR 1979 SC 391; Lakshmi Singh v. State of Bihar, AIR 1976 SC 2263; Jai Dev v. State of Punjab, AIR 1963 SC 612; Biran Singh v. State of Bihar, AIR 1975 SC 87; and Sekar v. State, (2002) 7 Supreme 124.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and private_defence_claimed and no_injuries_on_accused and serious_injuries_on_opposing_witness and not probable_defence_circumstances

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed against a criminal conviction.
predicates.private_defence_claimed: The accused claimed that the harm they caused was inflicted in private defence.
predicates.no_injuries_on_accused: The courts found that the accused had no injuries from the occurrence.
predicates.serious_injuries_on_opposing_witness: An opposing witness sustained numerous injuries and required prolonged hospitalisation.
predicates.probable_defence_circumstances: The evidence established circumstances making the private-defence account reasonably probable.
predicates.private_defence_claim_rejected: The claim that the accused acted in private defence is rejected.

issues.definition: When accused appealing their convictions claim private defence, have no injuries, and face evidence of serious injuries to an opposing witness without probable circumstances supporting the defence, the claim is rejected.

issues.legal_issue: The passage of time since an offence, by itself, does not justify reducing a sentence that is not harsh.
material_facts: The appellants sought reduced sentences, relying on the time elapsed since the occurrence and the time already served.
One appellant had already served the sentence imposed on him.
The Court found that the sentences imposed were not harsh.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to reduce the sentences and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The passage of time since the occurrence is not, by itself, a sufficient reason to reduce a sentence; the Court found the sentences in this case not harsh.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_sentence: The accused appealed against the sentence imposed in a criminal case.
predicates.sentence_not_harsh: The court found that the sentence imposed was not harsh.
predicates.elapsed_time_is_reduction_ground: The accused relied on the time elapsed since the occurrence as a reason to reduce the sentence.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a sentence the court finds not harsh and relies on elapsed time for a reduction, the sentence is not reduced.
